item.description: arXiv:2610.18320v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate that the symmetry of magnetoelastic coupling governs the topological organization of composite defects and can qualitatively alter phase-ordering kinetics. In a two-dimensional theory of an in-plane magnetic vector coupled to elastic strain, we find that integer magnetic vortices bind pairs of elementary elastic half-defects. Isotropic magnetostriction produces a core-induced elastic winding independent of the magnetic charge, giving defect binding without charge locking and leaving the magnetic sector with essentially XY-like coarsening. In contrast, quadrupolar magnetoelastic coupling locks magnetic and elastic defect charges: continuous rotational symmetry favors $q_\phi=q_\theta$, whereas crystalline anisotropy can reverse the locking to $q_\phi=-q_\theta$. We reveal that both locking sectors display anomalously slow vortex annihilation: defect density shows a power-law decay $t^{-2/5}$, while the average defect-velocity scales as $t^{-4/5}$. These results are consistent with a dynamic exponent $z\simeq 5$. We show that this coarsening slowdown is associated with large anisotropic elastic friction. An adiabatic elimination of the elastic field reveals that isotropic magnetostriction merely renormalizes local magnetic interactions, whereas orientational coupling induces effective nonlocal interactions between magnetic spins. Our experimentally testable results thus establish magnetoelastic coupling symmetry as a means of controlling defect topology and ordering kinetics.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Time-Resolved Phonon Dispersions of Thermally Excited Graphite at the Nanoscale
item.description: arXiv:2610.18561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice vibrations govern the propagation of heat in materials, and investigating their dynamics through time-resolved phonon dispersion measurements would provide insight into these excitations and their interactions. However, time-resolved measurements that directly resolve the phonon dispersion at the nanoscale have not been previously demonstrated. Momentum-resolved vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (EELS) provides access to phonon energies and momenta with nanoscale spatial resolution. Here, we combine momentum-resolved vibrational EELS with pulsed laser heating and synchronised gated electron detection to observe the phonon dispersion of graphite during controlled heating and cooling on the microsecond timescale. Recording both the gain and loss spectra at defined times relative to laser excitation, we determine the temperature at each time delay and follow changes to the phonon branches as a function of temperature. The momentum-resolved spectra reveal a decrease in energy of the optical phonon branch with increasing temperature accompanied by an increase in peak width. These changes are consistent with temperature-dependent phonon renormalisation and scattering associated with anharmonic interactions. The approach is compatible with detector gating on timescales down to 50 ns, providing a route towards extending these measurements to faster dynamics. This work demonstrates time-resolved phonon dispersion spectroscopy using vibrational EELS and provides a route towards probing temperature-dependent phonon dynamics at the nanoscale with simultaneous energy and momentum resolution.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Composition-controlled optical fingerprints and anisotropy of self-trapped excitons in double perovskites
item.description: arXiv:2610.18665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Double perovskites (DPs) offer a compositionally versatile platform for photocatalysis and optoelectronics, but their soft lattices favor strong exciton-phonon coupling and self-trapped excitons (STEs), which produce broad, red-shifted photoluminescence (PL). Here, we combine optical spectroscopy and ab initio calculations to study lead-free, Sb-doped Cs2BInCl6 nanocrystals with B-site alloying from Na to K. Alloying tunes the PL energy from about 2.48 to 2.70 eV, while absorption features near 3.8 eV remain nearly unchanged. Calculations reveal that Sb doping enables bright radiative recombination channels and delocalizes the excitonic wavefunction. We identify STEs responsible for the large PL red shift, associated with an upward shift of dopant-hybridized in-gap states. Na-to-K substitution selectively changes the STE lattice distortion, explaining why PL varies strongly with composition while absorption does not. Theory further predicts pronounced PL polarization anisotropy that reflects the STE wavefunction's spatial structure and depends on B-site composition. Time-resolved anisotropy measurements closely agree with these predictions, providing experimental fingerprints of the excitonic wavefunction and its evolution with alloying. Together, these results disentangle the roles of doping and alloying in lead-free DPs and establish polarization-resolved spectroscopy as a probe of STE wavefunctions.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Competing delocalisation and localisation induced by the dipolar tail in fragmented lattice gases
item.description: arXiv:2610.18747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate how the long-range tail of dipole-dipole interactions modifies the dynamics of strongly interacting hard-core bosons in a one-dimensional lattice. In the nearest-neighbour model, large interactions generate an emergent Hilbert-space fragmentation into manifolds labelled by the number of nearest-neighbour bonds \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\). The dipolar tail has a non-monotonic effect on this fragmented dynamics as the interaction-to-tunnelling ratio \(V/t\) is increased. At intermediate \(V/t\), it enhances delocalisation relative to the nearest-neighbour model by reducing the energetic detuning between neighbouring \(N_{\mathrm{NN}}\) manifolds and sustaining their hybridisation by hopping. At larger \(V/t\), the same tail lifts degeneracies within each manifold, beginning with the splitting associated with the next-nearest-neighbour bond number \(N_{\mathrm{NNN}}\), and promotes intra-manifold localisation and Hilbert-space shattering. The competition between these two effects produces a crossover from a delocalising to a localising role of the dipolar tail, visible in the late-time spatial inhomogeneity. This crossover occurs for nearly all initial states considered and persists at different fillings. Transverse confinement strengthens the short-range part of the dipolar tail and shifts the crossover to lower \(V/t\), bringing it into the regime relevant to current experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Spin textures at the Fermi surface of ferromagnets and associated torque
item.description: arXiv:2610.18800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish theoretically that transverse spin textures are generically induced by the spin-orbit interaction at the Fermi surface of centrosymmetric ferromagnetic metals. We confirm this prediction with {\em ab initio} computations for Fe, Co and Ni. By symmetry, this cannot be associated with spin-orbit torques under a uniform current. However, a new {\em current-gradient-induced} torque emerges in nanoscale geometries. For a series of Ni-based bilayers, the computed Ni thickness dependence of the current-gradient-induced torque is in quantitative agreement with measurements previously attributed to orbital torques. We discuss how this opens a new avenue for the electrical control of magnetic orders, possibly also including the N\'eel vector of metallic altermagnets.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Tracking Coupled Granular Temperature and Entropy Dynamics in Granular Materials via Dielectric Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2605.19560v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In glass-forming liquids, structural dynamics are governed by configurational entropy and temperature, with dielectric relaxation time scaling alongside structural relaxation time as described by the Adam-Gibbs (AG) model. Under Edwards's athermal statistical thermodynamics, a modified AG law similarly governs granular matter, provided that granular temperature and configurational entropy are appropriately defined. This study investigates whether variations in the structural relaxation of granular systems can be probed via thermally activated processes, specifically electric charge hopping and trapping. By progressively reducing the volume of graphite powder to vary its packing fraction, we estimated relative configurational entropy and granular temperature from volumetric data, while evaluating electrical conductivity and capacity via impedance spectroscopy. We demonstrate that the logarithm of the dielectric relaxation time, derived from complex impedance, scales with granular temperature and entropy across both loose and compact states. Consequently, changes in the complex impedance resulting from packing fraction variations are tuned by granule configuration, strictly adhering to an AG-like relationship for thermal systems. These findings establish dielectric spectroscopy as a viable, non-destructive tool for tracing configurational dynamics in granular matter, analogous to its established use in polymers and glass formers.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] A semi-infinite hydraulic fracture propagating in a poroelastic medium
item.description: arXiv:2610.14049v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We solve the near-tip coupled hydromechanical problem of a hydraulic fracture propagating in a permeable poroelastic medium, represented locally as a semi-infinite crack moving at constant velocity. In the moving tip frame, all fracture fields are steady. The porous solid obeys linear poroelasticity, fracture propagation follows LEFM, fluid flow within the tensile fracture is governed by lubrication theory, and the fracturing and pore fluids are treated as identical Newtonian liquids. The primary unknowns are the fracture opening and the fluid displacement function along the fracture, determined from the resulting non-linear system of equations. In a viscosity--toughness scaling, the problem depends on four dimensionless parameters: a dimensionless permeability $\varrho$ (associated with the intensity of fluid leak-in), a dimensionless effective confining stress $\Sigma_0'$ (measuring the relative importance of fluid leak-off and leak-in), the drained--undrained Poisson's ratio contrast $\beta$, and the poroelastic stress coefficient $\eta$. The solution evolves from a drained, toughness-dominated near-tip asymptote with uniform net pressure to an undrained, storage-viscosity-dominated far-field asymptote. Numerical solutions are obtained over parameter ranges representative of various rock types. The fully coupled model is compared with simplified models, namely uncoupled and one-way coupled formulations, over distances from the fracture front spanning laboratory-to-field scales. The resulting relative difference maps in the $(\varrho,\Sigma_0')$ parameter space identify four characteristic regimes: negligible poroelastic effects, dominance of the direct mechanical poroelastic response, importance of the poroelastic backstress, and a fully coupled regime. The latter occurs mainly at large $\varrho$ and small $\Sigma_0'$, corresponding to strong leak-in relative to leak-off.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Categorifying Quantum Spin Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.14165v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a homotopical framework for understanding the space of quantum spin systems based on topological $n$-nets, which assign associative unital algebras to local regions in an $n$-dimensional space in a manner that captures the locality structure of the underlying lattice theories. The net-theoretic perspective admits a natural categorification, in which the category of topological $n$-nets carries the structure of a higher Morita category. Moreover, the nets of greatest physical interest form a Karoubi-complete subcategory that shares many of the characteristic structural features of the category of finite TQFTs. Our main result identifies the group of locality-preserving symmetries of (3+1)-dimensional quantum spin systems (i.e. quantum cellular automata modulo stabilization, finite-depth quantum circuits, and translations) with the full Witt group of nondegenerate braided fusion categories, thereby answering a question posed by Haah.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Breakdown of thermalization in quantum spin systems with long-range interactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.15530v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum thermalization of closed systems -- i.e. the relaxation of local properties to their thermodynamic value along the Hamiltonian evolution -- is generically expected in non-integrable systems at finite energy density. In this work we show that quantum spin systems with at least one spin component coupled through long-range ferromagnetic interactions, and a second spin component coupled to a field, cannot in general thermalize to a paramagnetic state whenever they have a finite, negative energy per spin. The long-range interactions we consider decay as a power law of the distance, $\sim r^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha < d$, where $d$ is the number of spatial dimensions of the system. The lack of thermalization is generic to an infinite family of Hamiltonians, and it is not associated to any form of integrability. It can instead be understood by the anomalous features of the thermodynamics of the system in the paramagnetic phase, which cannot be reflected in the properties of the eigenstates. This leads to a breakdown of eigenstate typicality and of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Interestingly, the non-thermal states emerging at long times in the dynamics display long-range multipartite entanglement, elevating the breakdown of thermalization to a resource.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] From Lyapunov Growth to Weak Quantum Chaos
item.description: arXiv:2610.15880v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) measure the growth of initially small commutators. For bounded local operators, this growth ends when the local commutator becomes of order one, but in an extended system the region over which it is large can continue to expand. We study this spatial proliferation using three related observables: the local squared commutator $C_r(t)$, its spatial sum $\bar C(t) = \sum_r C_r(t)$, and the symmetrically regularised connected dOTOC $D(t)$ of two extensive observables. We show that Lieb--Robinson locality gives $\bar C(t) \lesssim t^d$. We then prove that, in a Gibbs state with uniform exponential clustering, the full dOTOC obeys the same bound, $D(t) \lesssim t^d$, improving our earlier suboptimal $t^{3d}$ bound. We illustrate these results in two quantum many-body systems: a Brownian coupled-cluster model and a finite-temperature SYK chain. In both cases, an exact disorder symmetry relates $D(t)$ to $\bar C(t)$ and allows us to follow the same extensive observable from the pre-scrambling Lyapunov regime into the post-scrambling growth associated with an expanding saturated region. This late-time power-law growth is the concrete realisation of the weak quantum chaos introduced in our earlier work.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Almost invariant subspaces in the topologically non-trivial setting: a pedestrian approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.16393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a self-contained, algorithmic construction of almost invariant subspaces [Panati et al. (2003), De Nittis and Panati (2010), Freund and Teufel (2016)] for Hofstadter-like Hamiltonians $H_b $ acting on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^2,\mathbb{C}^n)$. More precisely, for rational values of $b_0/(2\pi)$ we describe an iterative procedure that takes a ``locally gapped" projection $P_{0}$ (possibly topologically non-trivial) which commutes with $H_{b_0}$, into a projection $P_{\varepsilon}$ that commutes with $H_{b_0+\varepsilon}$ up to an error of order $\varepsilon^\infty$. Our construction insures that the Chern number of $P_{\varepsilon}$ equals the Chern number of $P_0$ as long as $P_\varepsilon$ exists. Moreover, its integrated density of states varies linearly with $\varepsilon$ (the ``St\v{r}eda formula"). We also show that any spatially localized Parseval frame of $P_{0}$ can be mapped into to a localized Parseval frame of $P_{\varepsilon}$. We choose to work with a discrete model in order to keep the technicalities to a minimum level, with no need for advanced pseudo-differential calculus. Nevertheless, we are confident that most of our results can be extended to (unbounded) magnetic (pseudo)differential operators, but the technical burden would be much heavier. This is left for future work.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Iterated Graph Systems (III): Alexander-Orbach conjecture on hierarchical lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.16875v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can the Alexander-Orbach conjecture hold on hierarchical lattices? We construct Gromov-Hausdorff-Prokhorov scaling limits of critical percolation clusters on hierarchical lattices in the chemical metric and determine the typical spectral dimensions of the associated diffusions. These dimensions are dense in $(1,2)$; however, outside a narrow region in dimension space, we prove that the Alexander-Orbach conjecture fails on every hierarchical lattice under consideration.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Elastic Properties of Titan Tholins Revealed by Brillouin Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.17564v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Titan tholins, complex organic solids synthesized by simulating photochemical processes in Titan's atmosphere, are widely regarded as analogs to organic surface materials on the Saturnian moon. Their mechanical properties are critical for understanding the evolution of Titan's geomorphology and crustal layering. Here, we report the first direct experimental determination of the complete set of aggregate elastic moduli of tholins using Brillouin spectroscopy. Measurements conducted on tholin powder samples yielded a bulk modulus of 11 (2) GPa and a shear modulus of 3.9 (5) GPa, from which we derive a Young's modulus of 11 (1) GPa and a Poisson's ratio of 0.34 (3). Thin-film samples synthesized under slightly different conditions yield similar results. Compared with other Titan-relevant organic compounds, tholins exhibit the highest elastic stiffness measured to date, exceeding even H2O ice in both bulk and shear moduli. These results support the interpretation that complex organics contribute significantly to the mechanical stability and transport behavior of Titan's equatorial dune sediments. Measurements following prolonged atmospheric exposure reveal persistent stiffening of tholins that remains after vacuum treatment, likely associated with minor chemical modification and physical reorganization, highlighting the importance of controlled sample handling for future laboratory investigations. This study also demonstrates the effectiveness of Brillouin spectroscopy as a non-destructive technique for characterizing planetary organic materials and provides new constraints relevant to future seismic and geophysical investigations by the Dragonfly mission.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Directed percolation in higher-order social dilemmas
item.description: arXiv:2610.18506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multiplayer social dilemmas on hypergraphs show a variety of emergent phenomena, which has been attributed to group interactions. Here we test whether pairwise dynamics can reproduce them as well. We derive the mesoscopic Langevin equation of a testbed model and find the operator content of absorbing phase transitions: a directed-percolation line, a tricritical point, and a first-order region whose spinodal is the explosive transition. In our analysis, three-player games only set the values of the Landau coefficients. We construct a strictly pairwise model with short-lived memory, in which every event involves at most two entities, that reproduces these coefficients term by term and has exactly the same mean-field fixed points. Simulations confirm that the two dynamics share mean-field critical and tricritical scaling and the size of the critical mass, and that a purely three-player game on a two-dimensional triangular lattice lies in the directed-percolation class. For these games, the explosive transition and the critical mass therefore do not require group interactions, and the critical behavior is that of the pairwise theory.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Fermion-fermion interaction driven phase transitions in rhombohedral trilayer graphene
item.description: arXiv:2406.01877v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The effects of short-range fermion-fermion interactions on the low-energy properties of rhombohedral trilayer graphene are comprehensively investigated using the momentum-shell renormalization group method. We take into account all one-loop corrections and establish the energy-dependent coupled evolutions of independent fermionic couplings that carry the physical information stemming from the interplay of various fermion-fermion interactions. With detailed numerical analysis, we observe that the ferocious competition among all fermion-fermion interactions can drive fermionic couplings to four distinct fixed points, dubbed $\textrm{FP}_{1}$, $\textrm{FP}_{2}$, $\textrm{FP}_{3}$, and $\textrm{FP}_{4}$, in the interaction-parameter space. These fixed points primarily dictate the fate of the system in the low-energy regime and are always associated with some instabilities characterized by specific symmetry breakings, leading to certain phase transitions. To determine the favorable states arising from the potential phase transitions, we introduce a number of fermion-bilinear source terms to characterize the underlying candidate states. By comparing their related susceptibilities, we find that the dominant states correspond to spin-singlet superconductivity, spin-triplet pair-density-waves, and spin-triplet superconductivity for fixed points $\textrm{FP}_{1,3}$, $\textrm{FP}_{2}$, and $\textrm{FP}_{4}$, respectively. These provide valuable insights into the low-energy properties of rhombohedral trilayer graphene and analogous materials.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Double circular dichroism high harmonic spectroscopy: An ultrafast probe for topological photocurrents
item.description: arXiv:2604.21121v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding optical responses of topological matter is central to optoelectronic applications, photocurrent control, and spectroscopy. Yet schemes for sensing ultrafast photocurrents and separating bulk and surface contributions are lacking. We introduce double circular dichroism (DCD) harmonic spectroscopy as an all-optical probe of ultrafast dynamics in topological materials. Pump and probe pulses are circular with independently controlled helicities, yielding the circular dichroism of the circular dichroism: a time-resolved response that evaluates how probe-induced dichroism depends on pump helicity. While DCD vanishes in symmetric systems, it survives in broken time-reversal-symmetry materials, including Chern insulators. Simulations in a Haldane nanoflake, where a pump manipulates chiral current-carrying states and intense probe pulses drive harmonic emission, show that DCD arises from bulk and edge-localized states with opposite signs, similar magnitudes, and different amplitude scaling. Edge-associated DCD is connected to the outermost atomic layer of exponentially localized protected modes and is relatively robust to bulk-edge interference, enabling separation of bulk and edge photocurrents. Varying the electronic structure and laser parameters reveals harmonic anomalies that may probe topological attributes of photocurrents and material phase. In particular, HHG DCD oscillations under band-structure manipulation vary strongly across the phase transition and become stable and nonoscillatory in topologically trivial phases. DCD also oscillates with pump-probe delay on attosecond timescales, offering an ultrafast probe of topological photocurrents and their coherence. DCD could therefore disentangle bulk and boundary photoresponses in broken-symmetry quantum and topological matter and be implemented in photoelectron and absorption pump-probe spectroscopies and chiral systems.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Discrete Lattice Models for Interface Growth on a Complete Graph
item.description: arXiv:2604.27896v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the behavior of discrete interface growth models belonging to the Edwards--Wilkinson (EW) and Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) universality classes, when defined on a complete graph, a topology commonly used to probe the infinite-dimensional limit of statistical mechanical systems. Our aim is to assess to what extent discrete lattice models reproduce the behavior of their corresponding continuum equations in this highly connected setting. After assessing the trivial behavior shown by some well known cases (like random deposition with surface relaxation or the etching model), we focus on two paradigmatic models associated with the KPZ universality class, the Restricted Solid-on-Solid (RSOS) and Ballistic Deposition (BD) models, and assess non-trivial behavior through several observables including the roughness, height fluctuations, power spectra, and two-time autocorrelation functions. Still, despite similarities with continuum equations, important differences arise in the fluctuations and long-time dynamics. In both discrete models the rescaled height fluctuations display a pronounced left tail, indicating the presence of lagging nodes. While the RSOS model exhibits a saturation roughness that decreases with system size, similarly to the EW and KPZ equations, the BD model exhibits a saturation roughness that increases with system size and an additional ultrafast growth regime, placing it outside the KPZ universality class on a complete graph.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Boundary-dependent topological degeneracy in an Ising chain
item.description: arXiv:2605.09510v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The influence of boundary conditions on bulk properties is generally expected to vanish in the thermodynamic limit. Here we show that this expectation can fail in an open transverse field Ising chain with modified boundary fields. By removing only the transverse fields acting on the two edge spins while leaving the bulk Hamiltonian unchanged, we uncover a boundary-induced switching of the topological spectral degeneracy. In contrast to the conventional open chain, where the topological degeneracy occurs in the ferromagnetic phase ($\left\vert g\right\vert <1$), the modified boundary condition shifts it to the paramagnetic phase ($\left\vert g\right\vert >1$). We demonstrate that the underlying mechanism originates from two exact local conserved quantities associated with the edge spins, which partition the Hilbert space into invariant sectors. Based on this structure, we establish an exact description in terms of domain-wall excitations, under which the Hamiltonian decomposes into two independent Kitaev chains. Complementarily, the Majorana representation reveals that the spectral switching originates from different unit-cell conventions and boundary terminations of the corresponding effective SSH lattice, leading to distinct boundary zero-mode structures without altering the bulk Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we show that the boundary-induced topological degeneracy remains observable at finite temperatures through non-Hermitian quench dynamics, providing a dynamical manifestation of the bulk-boundary correspondence. These results demonstrate that boundary engineering, through the introduction of local conserved boundary degrees of freedom, provides an effective route for controlling topological degeneracy in quantum spin chains without modifying bulk interactions.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Nambu Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics and the Lyapunov Structure of Open Systems
item.description: arXiv:2606.05231v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the thermodynamic meaning of the dissipation potential in Nambu nonequilibrium thermodynamics (NNET) using a simple open-piston model. The system is described by three variables: the gas volume, the piston momentum, and the thermodynamic entropy of the gas. The reversible dynamics is formulated in terms of two Nambu Hamiltonians, the extended energy and the thermodynamic entropy, while the irreversible dynamics is generated by a bath-relative Massieu-type dissipation potential through a positive-semidefinite gradient flow. This construction reproduces the physical processes of frictional heating and heat exchange with the reservoir while preserving their thermodynamic interpretation. We show that the time derivative of the dissipation potential coincides with the total entropy production rate of the system and the heat bath. Although the subsystem entropy may evolve nonmonotonically, the dissipation potential is a Lyapunov function under the conditions realized in this model. These results provide an explicit thermodynamic interpretation of the dissipation potential and its associated Lyapunov structure within NNET.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Anderson localization on the Bethe lattice
item.description: arXiv:2606.24671v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Anderson localization - the suppression of wave propagation by interference in a sufficiently disordered medium - is one of the most remarkable phenomena in condensed matter physics. These lecture notes provide a pedagogical introduction to Anderson localization on the Bethe lattice, an infinite tree with fixed connectivity and no loops, and one of the few settings in which the transition can be studied exactly. The problem is important for two main reasons. First, the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice provides a mean-field, infinite-dimensional limit in which the transition point and critical behavior can be determined exactly. Second, it provides a simplified description of the high-dimensional configuration spaces of interacting quantum systems, and thus a useful toy model for many-body localization. We focus on the Green's function formalism and the cavity method. After recalling standard diagnostics of localization based on transport, spectral statistics, and eigenfunction moments, we show that they are encoded in the statistics of the Green's functions, and that the full distribution of the local density of states is the natural order parameter of the transition. We derive the exact self-consistent cavity equations on the Bethe lattice, use them to characterize the two phases and critical behavior - including an analytic solution at large connectivity - and describe population-dynamics algorithms that solve them with high precision. We explain how an exponentially large correlation volume and the localized nature of the critical point account for the strong finite-size effects on random regular graphs, which led to a long debate over a possible intermediate non-ergodic phase. Finally, we discuss the mapping onto directed polymers in random media, interpreting localization as a freezing transition dominated by a few rare resonant paths.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Preconditioning Magnetic Systems in Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory
item.description: arXiv:2606.26693v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The convergence of the self-consistent field iterations in Kohn-Sham density functional theory can be significantly hindered by the presence of small eigenvalues in the dielectric matrix, which are often associated with electronic phase transitions in magnetic systems. In this work, we study this type of convergence issues and propose a new preconditioning scheme to mitigate them. Our preconditioning scheme is inspired by the Stoner model and based on a non-interacting susceptibility that neglects orbital variations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a range of ferromagnetic systems, showing that it can significantly reduce the number of iterations required to achieve convergence in the vicinity of magnetic phase transitions.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Negative charging energy in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ quantum dots induced by SrTiO$_3$ polarization
item.description: arXiv:2610.07878v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a microscopic mechanism for the negative charging energy in LaAlO$_3$/SrTiO$_3$ quantum dots, arising from the electrostatic image charge associated with the paraelectric response of SrTiO$_3$. Using a self-consistent configuration-interaction approach that accounts for both Coulomb repulsion and image-charge interactions, we find a robust regime of electron pairing whose strength is tunable through the confinement potential and the effective image-charge distance, set by the thickness of the interfacial two-dimensional electron gas. Our results establish dielectric image-charge effects as a route to controllable electron pairing in oxide quantum dots and other materials with a strong dielectric response.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Correspondence between Asymptotic Quantum Many-Body Scars in Closed Systems and Diffusive Nambu-Goldstone Modes in Open Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.09662v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hydrodynamic relaxation in open quantum many-body systems can be understood in terms of diffusive Nambu--Goldstone (NG) modes associated with strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB). Here, we find a common structure underlying weak ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems and diffusive hydrodynamics in open quantum systems. We establish a spectral correspondence between the parent Hamiltonian of rainbow quantum many-body scar (RQMBS) states in closed systems and the effective Lindbladian of strongly dissipative open systems with strong $U(1)$ symmetry and local charge-dephasing Lindblad operators. For broad classes of spin, fermionic, and bosonic systems, we construct asymptotic RQMBS (ARQMBS) states. Within the enlarged scar subspace, the parent Hamiltonian admits a local Rokhsar--Kivelson-type frustration-free decomposition. A single-mode variational construction gives an $O(k^2)$ upper bound on its lowest excitation energy and yields states satisfying the defining ARQMBS criteria: orthogonality, vanishing energy variance, and characteristic entanglement scaling. Under vectorization, RQMBS states are mapped to maximally mixed infinite-temperature states in fixed-charge sectors, which exhibit long-range SWSSB order under finite-density conditions. Assuming uniformly bounded positive transition rates, the effective Lindbladian has the same local projectors as the parent Hamiltonian but with positive transition-dependent weights, yielding two-sided spectral bounds and the same system-size scaling of their gaps. For uniform rates, the two operators are proportional to each other and their eigenmodes coincide. Therefore, an exact quadratic parent-Hamiltonian branch maps directly to a diffusive NG mode. Our results connect different mechanisms of slow relaxation in closed and open quantum many-body systems.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Prediction of the thermal neutron response of grain-boundary impedance in Gd-doped ceria based on the radiation-ionic effect
item.description: arXiv:2610.10191v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The radiation-ionic effect was recently reported in 3 mol% Gd-doped CeO$_2$ (3GDC): under $^{60}$Co gamma irradiation at 35 Gy/min, the grain-boundary (GB) ionic resistance of a bulk pellet decreased 680-fold at room temperature, because electrons trapped at the GB core lower the space-charge potential. The effect has been demonstrated only with photons. Gd has the largest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable element and is also the dopant that creates the GB barrier in GDC, so the same mechanism could link GB impedance to thermal-neutron sensing; whether it does, and under what conditions, has not been examined. Here the thermal-neutron response of 3GDC is modelled with the gamma-calibrated Mott-Schottky/Seager framework, with unmeasured parameters carried as intervals and propagated jointly. Each capture deposits about 50 keV by conversion and Auger electrons within 1 $\mu$m, the remaining 8 MeV leaving as prompt photons; Gd segregation to the GBs adds a factor of only 1-2 because the electron range exceeds the grain size. A thermal flux of $8\times10^{9}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$ (6-12$\times10^{9}$) matches the GB-effective generation rate of the 35 Gy/min calibration, and the predicted room-temperature GB resistance ratio is 110 (70-170) at $10^{9}$ and 970 (600-1500) at $10^{10}$ cm$^{-2}$s$^{-1}$, falling to 2 at 61 (55-68) and 81 (73-92) $^\circ$C. The neutron case differs from gamma irradiation in three respects: capture events are discrete, so the continuous-source approximation depends on the unmeasured trapped-charge lifetime; self-shielding (mean free path 0.27 mm) makes the response thickness dependent; and capture photons absorbed in the pellet add a gamma term comparable to the local term for pellets of 0.3 mm or more. The intervals are conditional on the model and exclude its structural error. The conditions under which the prediction can be tested are given.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Spin-Based Modeling of Perception as Emergent from contextualized Internal Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2507.06041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a microscopic model of perception of an interoceptive sensation in which spin-like variables encode an organism's internal evaluation of embodied vital norms associated with the sensation. Spins can take positive, negative, or neutral values. These local valorizations interact on a lattice embedded in the environmental context, and their collective configuration gives rise to a macroscopic perceptual state. By applying a coarse-graining procedure to a family of symmetric spin models, we derive a macroscopic Landau-type functional that makes explicit the mechanism by which key phenomenological features of perception, emerge from microscopic evaluative interactions. A central result is that the inclusion of a neutral evaluative state fundamentally alters the structure of the perceptual landscape, enhancing entropy, lowering the critical threshold, and increasing sensitivity to contextual input. These results establish a principled link between microscopic evaluative processes and large-scale perceptual organization, offering a flexible framework for integrating perceptual regulation and neurobiological modeling. The model integrates notions of neuroscience and cognitive science using the formalism of condensed matter field theory and providing novel theoretical insights and experimental predictions for conditions such as mental disorders and chronic pain.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Symmetric Gapped States and Symmetry-Enforced Gaplessness in 3-dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2602.12335v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish a comprehensive framework for characterizing the infrared (IR) phases of a fermionic quantum theory in three spatial dimensions, based on its quantum anomalies associated with a finite symmetry. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy among these anomalies: the first class of anomalies can always be realized by symmetric gapped states, while the second class can never be realized by gapped states without breaking the given symmetry, establishing the phenomenon of symmetry-enforced gaplessness in these settings. Moreover, using the construction of symmetry extension, we construct the candidate gapped states that theories with the first class of anomalies can flow to in the IR. As an application, we provide concrete predictions of the candidate IR phases of (3+1)-dimensional gauge theories based on our results. Our results also suggest that systems with discrete chiral anomalies cannot be gapped out by adding arbitrary bosonic degrees of freedom.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Phase diagram of a lattice fermion model with symmetric mass generation
item.description: arXiv:2602.18360v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the phase structure of a model containing two flavors of massless staggered fermions interacting through two independent four-fermion couplings, UI and UB, formulated on a three-dimensional Euclidean space-time lattice. At UB = 0, this model is known to exhibit a direct second-order quantum phase transition between a massless fermion (MF) phase and a phase in which fermions acquire masses through the mechanism commonly referred to as symmetric mass generation (SMG). We demonstrate that introducing a small nonzero value of UB qualitatively alters this structure: the single exotic transition at UB = 0 splits into two distinct, conventional transitions, separated by an intermediate phase in which fermion masses arise through the standard mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB). The first of these is a Gross-Neveu transition separating the MF phase from the SSB-induced massive phase, while the second is a three-dimensional XY transition between the SSB phase and the SMG phase. Using the fermion-bag Monte Carlo method, we verify that the critical exponents associated with both transitions are consistent with the literature, thereby yielding a quantitative characterization of the resulting phase structure of the model.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Entanglement Growth from Structured Initial States in Many-Body Localized Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.20656v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Understanding how complex entanglement structures emerge is a central problem in quantum many-body physics. Recent work by Zhang et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 020404 (2026)] has considered structured initial states prepared by evolving a product state under a chaotic Hamiltonian for a finite time before quenching to the target Hamiltonian. In this setup, total entanglement entropy growth in many-body localized systems exhibits two distinct regimes, first increasing and then decreasing as the initial entanglement is tuned. In this work, we identify the physical origin of this behavior by analyzing the dynamics of both the R\'enyi entanglement entropy and the Wehrl-R\'enyi entropy in the random-field XXZ model, the latter of which characterizes multipartite entanglement. We show that a similar non-monotonic dependence on the initial entanglement also appears in the net growth of the Wehrl-R\'enyi entropy for product states polarized along the $z$-direction. The first regime is governed by a finite magnetization associated with local integrals of motion, while the second reflects inter-site correlations. In contrast, for product states in the $x/y$-direction, the entanglement growth exhibits a monotonic decay. Our results provide a more fine-grained picture of how distinct initial-state properties shape entanglement dynamics in many-body localized systems.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] Beyond Calabrese-Cardy Scaling: Exceptional-Point Sensitivity and the de Sitter RT Surface
item.description: arXiv:2607.21536v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Entanglement entropy at one-dimensional criticality typically follows the Calabrese--Cardy scaling. In the non-Hermitian critical free-fermion systems studied here, however, we find an additional interval-independent contribution $S_{\rm res}=\log(\Delta L)$, which allows the entropy to remain sensitive to energy gaps below the finite-size scale, $\Delta<1/L$. We refer to this term as the residual entropy. To understand its infrared origin, we examine finite-depth non-unitary continuous multiscale entanglement renormalization on a ring. Terminating the critical RG circuit before its singular final layer leaves a two-site infrared state. We calculate the entropy of this state directly from its correlation matrix and recover the same \(\log(\Delta L)\) dependence. The emergent de Sitter geometry provides a complementary geometric interpretation: extremal curves associated with different boundary intervals extend to a common infrared endpoint, suggesting how the entanglement retained there can contribute equally to their entropies.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cond-mat updates on arXiv.org] A strategic roadmap for an atomistic machine-learning ecosystem
item.description: arXiv:2609.39090v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data-driven machine learning (ML) techniques have become an essential tool in many domains of science. Their application to atomistic simulations of matter is particularly widespread and impactful. This success is due largely to the existence of a well-developed and established physics-based modeling framework, ranging from first-principles electronic-structure calculations to molecular dynamics and statistical sampling, into which ML was integrated naturally to reshape long-standing trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, and scale. Nevertheless, this integration raises both conceptual and practical challenges, from choosing between data-centric and physics-based modeling approaches to adapting established software stacks to modern hardware accelerators and ML libraries. As the field evolves rapidly, fueled in part by widespread enthusiasm but also by tangible impact, it seems appropriate to take a moment to consider the current state of the art and open challenges, and reflect on what can be done to better coordinate efforts across the community. With this goal in mind, several members of this community met in Lausanne in January 2026 at CECAM to discuss algorithms, models, software and hardware infrastructure, and the most promising scientific applications that have become possible thanks to the use of artificial intelligence in atomic-scale simulations. This strategic roadmap paper summarizes the outcomes of these discussions, suggesting some long-term goals, and some concrete actions, to establish a healthy, sustainable and impactful atomistic ML ecosystem.
item.author: cond-mat updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] Programmable Data Layouts via On-The-Fly Data Transformation
item.description: arXiv:2610.15193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The performance of modern computing systems is heavily bottlenecked by the widening gap between processing throughput and main memory latency, a problem exacerbated when an application's logical data access patterns misalign with the physical layout of data in memory. To address this, we propose a hardware-software co-design framework comprising the Data Transformation Language (DTL) and the Data Transformation Unit (DTU). DTL allows programmers to concisely express complex data layout reorganizations, which the compiler translates into efficient hardware routing configurations. The DTU, a hardware engine logically situated between the Last-Level Cache (LLC) and main memory, transparently evaluates these configurations on-the-fly to gather scattered data elements into dense, logically contiguous cache lines. By converting explicit layout transformations into virtual views, this approach eliminates the need for explicit data materialization in software. We evaluate the DTU within a quad-core RISC-V SoC using FireSim, demonstrating substantial improvements in execution speed and memory efficiency.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.15205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] The Era of Vibe Tapeout: Dark Age or Golden Age for Analog Circuit Design?
item.description: arXiv:2610.15240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents now write their own schematic and layout generators, run EDA tools, read the results, and fix the design. This "vibe tapeout" is becoming practical for analog circuits as well. This paper measures how far it has come in two settings. (A) On an open PDK (SKY130), a cloud LLM agent designed an 11-bit, 5.12-MS/s SAR ADC from its specification. The agents produced DRC- and LVS-clean macros and met the specification after parasitic extraction (PEX). In particular, under the condition in which the agent received a sanitized reference design derived from our 65-nm design (vibe porting), it produced the best layout in the shortest time. Its area was 1/1.6 to 1/2.8 of that of the conditions without a reference. This condition reached signoff without human intervention. The agents also identified the causes of post-PEX degradation (CDAC wiring coupling and common-mode-dependent comparator offset) by their own experiments. On the other hand, agents sometimes reported false passes, and verification independent of the design agent was essential. (B) A commercial PDK is under NDA and cannot be given to a cloud LLM. We therefore evaluated local LLMs running on university servers with a six-task benchmark on a commercial 65-nm CMOS PDK. Kimi K3 passed five of the six tasks, while MiniMax M3 passed two. Neither solved the debugging task, which requires finding the cause from symptoms. Finally, we discuss the prospects for extending vibe tapeout from ADCs to entire SoCs, and ask whether vibe tapeout is a dark age or a golden age for analog design. Our answer is that it is a golden age for designers who know what to verify.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] GarageWorks: A Shared Testbench Abstraction for Software Simulation and FPGA Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.15925v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GarageWorks is a lightweight FPGA testing framework that enables the same cocotb testbench to be used for both software RTL simulation and FPGA-accelerated hardware simulation. A shared abstraction hides backend-specific interfaces, while synthesizable Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) dispatchers provide design-under-test (DUT)-specific control and test operations on the FPGA. GarageWorks is intended for rapid bare-metal testing of standalone designs and on-chip processing logic for scientific sensors, rather than full SoC-level prototyping. The framework has been validated on AMD Alveo V80 FPGAs with several internal designs and provides initial support for AI-assisted generation of DUT-specific test components.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
item.description: arXiv:2610.17099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] FPGA Based Design And Implementation of Neural Network Compensators for Nanocrystalline MEMS Pressure Sensor
item.description: arXiv:2610.18136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper the effects of nonlinearity and temperature of nanocrystalline MEMS pressure sensor have been compensated using neural network algorithm which has been implemented on a FPGA chip. The neural network employs back propagation algorithm to train the multilayer perceptron feed forward network that causes an error reduction due to temperature upto the level of 98%. It is realized on FPGA with pipelined architecture for parallel and fast sensing operation. The pressure sensor along with the FPGA based compensation results in an intelligent sensor system capable of high speed and accurate pressure measurement which has been tested for a typical biomedical application.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerators for Space Applications: A Survey
item.description: arXiv:2504.16173v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Space missions are becoming increasingly ambitious, necessitating high-performance onboard spacecraft computing systems. In response, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) have garnered significant interest due to their flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and radiation tolerance potential. Concurrently, neural networks (NNs) are being recognized for their capability to execute space mission tasks such as autonomous operations, sensor data analysis, and data compression. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to implement FPGA-based NN accelerators in space applications. By analyzing existing literature, identifying trends and gaps, and proposing future research directions, this work highlights the potential of these accelerators to enhance onboard computing systems.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] RISC-Q: A Generator for Real-Time Quantum Control System-on-Chips Compatible with RISC-V
item.description: arXiv:2505.14902v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum computing imposes stringent requirements for the precise control of large-scale qubit systems, including, for example, microsecond-latency feedback and nanosecond-precision timing of gigahertz signals-demands that far exceed the capabilities of conventional real-time systems. The rapidly evolving and highly diverse nature of quantum control necessitates the development of specialized hardware accelerators. While a few custom real-time systems have been developed to meet the tight timing constraints of specific quantum platforms, they face major challenges in scaling and adapting to increasingly complex control demands-largely due to fragmented toolchains and limited support for design automation. To address these limitations, we present RISC-Q---an open-source flexible generator for Quantum Control System-on-Chip (QCSoC) designs, featuring a programming interface compatible with the RISC-V ecosystem. Developed using SpinalHDL, RISC-Q enables efficient automation of highly parameterized and modular QCSoC architectures, supporting agile and iterative development to meet the evolving demands of quantum control. We demonstrate that RISC-Q can replicate the performance of existing QCSoCs with significantly reduced development effort, facilitating efficient exploration of the hardware-software co-design space for rapid prototyping and customization.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] LowRank-SSM: Hardware-Software Co-Design for Rank-Reduced Mamba Acceleration on FPGA
item.description: arXiv:2608.02954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba and Mamba-2 achieve linear-time autoregressive inference, making them attractive for latency-sensitive and resource-constrained deployment. Yet every generated token still reads the full input and output projection weights of every layer from off-chip memory, and on an FPGA these two projections take the majority of a layer's cycles. Existing accelerators lower this cost by quantizing the weights or by speeding up the scan, but none reduce the number of weight elements a token must read, and a low-rank factorization on its own does not help: without a datapath built for it, the two-stage product takes as long as the dense one. We present \textbf{LowRank-SSM}, a hardware-software co-design framework that jointly addresses three constraints of rank-reduced Mamba inference: where rank should be spent, how the resulting factors should execute, and how reduced weight traffic should be delivered by the FPGA memory system. A sensitivity-guided per-projection search allocates rank under a perplexity ceiling while restricting compression to Mamba-2 operands that tolerate approximation. A rank-configurable projection datapath maps both factor stages onto the existing GEMV engines, keeping the intermediate vector on chip and changing rank through loop bounds and weight images rather than bitstream recompilation. A platform-aware NoC/AXI memory subsystem then balances and prefetches weight streams to sustain 42\,GB/s. Together, these software and hardware choices convert structural rank reduction into measured latency reduction: in our ablation, 93\% of the projection traffic removed by rank reduction appears as saved token latency. With a rank schedule found under a 5\% perplexity ceiling, which costs 1.6 points of average zero-shot accuracy, the complete accelerator decodes Mamba2-2.7B at 16.79 tokens/s and 0.41\,J per token.
item.author: cs.AR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs.AR updates on arXiv.org] Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.05062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference outside the design point of LLM serving systems. Although VLA architectures combine familiar vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, their runtime behavior in this batch-1 control setting remains uncharacterized. We characterize four representative VLA models on an edge GPU server and two onboard SoCs, using single-inference profiling and 43,200 closed-loop episodes. Action tensor dimensionality determines whether a stage is memory- or compute-bound, platform balance can shift that bottleneck, and GPU frequency scaling yields a platform-dependent energy-latency sweet spot. In closed-loop operation, overlapping inference with action execution creates an accuracy-speed-energy tradeoff, and no configuration is Pareto-dominant across deployment SLOs. These results guide joint design of VLA model architectures, hardware, and runtime policies.

item.title: [Applied Physics Letters Current Issue] Energy dissipation in silicon MEMS resonators with varying thicknesses of aluminum layers
item.description: The influence of thin aluminum layers on the dissipation mechanisms of silicon microresonators is systematically studied in relation to metal-layer thickness. Quality factor measurements are performed at the wafer level using an automated setup, with each thickness variation tested on approximately 100 resonators to ensure statistical robustness and high throughput. The results show that additional dissipation from the aluminum layers can be effectively described with an isotropic loss factor. A clear correlation exists between the quality factor and metal thickness: negligible impact for ultra-thin (10 nm), discontinuous layers, but a significant decrease for continuous layers that intensifies with increasing thickness (up to 636 nm). Using a numerical model, we find that the dissipation associated with the metal layer is characterized by a mean isotropic loss parameter η=6.53 Pa/kPa constant over a broad range of thicknesses. These results provide a quantitative understanding of the thickness-dependent damping in aluminum-coated silicon microelectromechanical systems resonators and highlight the importance of considering metal-layer losses in high-Q devices used for sensing, timing, and related applications.

item.title: [Applied Physics Letters Current Issue] Spatially sequenced humidification decouples ionization and ozone chemistry in a floating-electrode plasma jet
item.description: Adding H2O to atmospheric-pressure plasma jets can suppress ozone (O3) but also attenuate the discharge that generates reactive species. We examine whether downstream H2O injection can separate these effects in a floating-electrode tube atmospheric-pressure plasma jet. Transient fluid simulations, optical diagnostics, gas- and liquid-phase measurements, and GL261 cell assays show that inlet H2O increases channel impedance and weakens floating-electrode charging and ionization-wave propagation through electron-energy loss, attachment, and excited-He quenching. By contrast, the same nominal H2O load injected downstream preserves the upstream conductive channel and second ionization wave while redirecting effluent chemistry. Relative to Dry-He, downstream injection reduces gas-phase O3 by more than 90%, retains approximately 93% of the He I emission and 90% of the liquid-phase DCFH response, and produces the highest mean intracellular DCFH signal. Separating energy deposition from H2O-mediated chemistry thus enables low-O3 operation without global discharge attenuation.

item.title: [Applied Physics Letters Current Issue] Josephson parametric amplifier with third-order resonator impedance matching
item.description: We propose and realize a multi-resonator coupled impedance-matched Josephson parametric amplifier. Parallel plate capacitors serve as couplers to achieve coupling between the nonlinear resonator containing the Josephson loop and the half-wavelength resonator, and between the half-wavelength resonators themselves. By precisely designing each coupling strength, we effectively extend the amplifier's bandwidth. Through a combination of circuit-level and electromagnetic field simulations, we optimize the structural parameters of the resonators and capacitors. The two measured devices have 15 dB gain with a bandwidth of 1.3 GHz and 20 dB gain with a bandwidth of 1.1 GHz, respectively, with near-quantum-limited noise temperatures.

item.title: [Applied Physics Letters Current Issue] Ultrasound real-time imaging of crack propagation during ultrasonic fatigue tests
item.description: This Letter describes a real-time surface inspection method based on ultrasonic synthetic imaging using Rayleigh waves. The proposed method can be employed to monitor crack propagation during ultrasonic fatigue tests. The setup, which is highly sensitive to cracks, enables the imaging of a large surface (tens of mm2), with spatial resolutions of several tens of micrometers and an imaging frequency of up to 50 frames per second. The micrometric resolution allows cracks to be investigated at the grain level, while the sample imaging enables high-velocity crack propagation to be accurately resolved. These two domains have rarely been investigated to date because of experimental limitations. This work paves the way for a new type of laboratory-scale fatigue monitoring based on crack propagation, leading to better comprehension of the associated physical phenomena.
item.author: Applied Physics Letters Current Issue

item.title: [Applied Physics Reviews Current Issue] Nanoscale petabyte optical memories: Past, present, and beyond
item.description: Human society has entered a rapidly evolving, intelligence-driven information age. The swift advancement of information technologies, such as big data and large-scale AI models, generates immense demand for information processing and data storage capabilities, accompanied by significant corresponding challenges. Existing data centers, built upon traditional electromagnetic storage technology, exhibit substantial limitations in terms of data storage capacity, energy consumption, cost, and sustainability. Optical data storage, with its unique advantages such as low energy consumption, cost-effectiveness, and long-term data preservation, presents a highly promising solution to the data storage demands and challenges of both the present and the future. After the background introduction, this review first introduces the development of commercial optical storage technology and summarizes its limitations. The advancements in nanophotonics technology, including super-resolution microscopy, nanolithography, and nanomaterials, are then reviewed as the basis for developing nanoscale optical storage technology. This review proceeds with a comprehensive discussion of the major technical pathways for developing high-capacity optical storage technologies: multidimensional optical storage, holographic optical storage, and super-resolution optical storage technology. Several aspects are then proposed regarding the development of the next generation petabyte intelligent optical memory technology envisioned as the future direction. Finally, this review gives a brief summary and proposes an outlook on collaborative efforts across industries to tackle the needs and challenges of optical storage technology in the AI-driven era.
item.author: Applied Physics Reviews Current Issue
